column1: Mimicking

What is the belief of atheists regarding the explanation of everything through science? Is there a possibility of something beyond explanation according to atheists? This is a fascinating question, and it reveals a lot about the core tenants of atheism. Atheists, by definition, do not believe in the existence of a god or any supernatural entity. Therefore, when it comes to explaining the universe and everything in it, they generally rely on the tools and methods of science. Science, in its essence, is the process of observation, experimentation, and the formulation of testable hypotheses to understand the natural world. For atheists, science offers the most reliable and evidence-based framework for comprehending how things work.So, do atheists believe that everything can be explained by science? That’s a tricky one. While science has made tremendous strides in explaining the universe, including the origins of the cosmos, the development of life, and the intricacies of human consciousness, it’s also constantly evolving. New discoveries are always being made, and our understanding is always being refined. However, science can only explain what can be observed or measured, and there is always a possibility that there are things beyond explanation, at least with our current capabilities. For many atheists, the possibility of something currently unexplainable doesn't necessarily negate the scientific method; it just means we don't yet have the tools or knowledge to understand it. Furthermore, a non-explanation isn't necessarily proof of a God or something supernatural. The universe is vast and complex, and there's always the potential for discoveries that will change how we see things. The key is to remain open-minded, embrace skepticism, and continue to follow wherever credible evidence leads.

Atheists, isn't your Darwinian theory a little far-fetched when you think about it? The theory states that all living things have a common ancestor. An elephant and a mosquito share a common ancestor? Really? Wow, the thought of an evolutionary lineage stretching that far is pretty wild, I'll give you that. But it's not like Darwin or anyone else just pulled that idea out of thin air. The evidence is all around us, if you know where to look. Now, I'm no biologist, and I'm not gonna try to explain it all in detail - there are plenty of textbooks and documentaries that can do a way better job than I could. But the basic idea is that organisms change over time, and that these changes are passed down to their offspring. Over vast stretches of time, these tiny changes can add up to some pretty big differences between the descendants and the ancestors. It's like a game of telephone, but instead of words, it's genetic material, and the results get more and more different with each generation. And the elephant and the mosquito? Yeah, they're related. It's just that their common ancestor was so far back in the evolutionary timeline that it's almost impossible for us to truly visualize, but that doesn't mean it didn't exist.

Do they still teach the myth about Columbus being the first European to reach the Americas in US schools? I don't know if they still teach it, but the claim is, of course, completely bogus. The Vikings beat him by several centuries. And it's important to point out that the Vikings weren't even the first to find it. Archeological evidence points to at least one, and possibly multiple, pre-Viking encounters with the Americas from somewhere in the North Atlantic. I'd heard about the evidence before, but I really started to look into it after a friend of mine mentioned this Quora question: ABOVE SOURCE: Did the Vikings discover America before Christopher Columbus? It’s a really, really common question on Quora, and there are a lot of great answers to it. They talk all about the various archaeological sites and about how they show that there were definitely settlements there hundreds of years before Columbus ever set sail. Of course, Columbus never actually set foot on what we now call the United States anyway. He landed in the Bahamas. But even then, he wasn't first to find the Bahamas. The people who lived there beat him by centuries, too. So anyway, to answer the question, the Columbus myth, like so many other myths, is a bunch of bunk.

Is it considered rude to be served on paper plates and plastic utensils at a dinner party? That's a fair question, and it really depends on a few things. The most important would be what kind of dinner party we’re talking about. If it's a casual get-together, a backyard barbecue or something along those lines, then paper plates and plastic utensils are perfectly acceptable. They’re easy, they're convenient, and people aren't expecting a gourmet, formal affair. This is the sort of thing where you can just roll up with a six-pack of beer or soda and a bag of chips and nobody's the wiser. But if it’s a more formal dinner party, a sit-down meal with multiple courses, then paper plates and plastic utensils would be, yes, considered a faux pas. It would show a lack of care and attention to detail, a sense that the host hasn’t really put much thought into the experience of their guests. You’d probably get better results and a much more positive reaction if you used, oh, I don't know, *actual* plates and silverware. Some people might argue that it's rude, period, regardless of how casual it is, and they might have a point. After all, it's not that difficult to wash dishes by hand. Still, there's a wide spectrum of responses you'd likely get. And even if you're trying to be casual and it is supposed to be a simple backyard party, some people might still consider it rude. They'll definitely realize that you went the cheap route at the expense of comfort.

Are atheists truly correct if everything has to have a creator? The Earth can't come out of nothingness. It had to be created by something. This argument seems superficially logical, but it's a bit of a non sequitur. It's not necessarily the case that because something exists, it *must* have a creator. And furthermore, even if the universe did have a creator, that creator wouldn't necessarily need to be a "God" in any of the ways that word is commonly defined. It could just be some other natural force or something beyond our current ability to understand. I’ve never understood the argument that just because *we* can't personally understand where something came from, that the answer has to automatically be God - a concept that itself is incredibly convoluted and often incomprehensible. The universe doesn’t care what our feelings regarding how much we understand about it are, or whether or not we believe in it. The fact that it is beyond our current comprehension doesn’t mean that the answer is *automatically* a supernatural something. We've all heard the answer that the Universe and all of its laws were created by the hands of God. But given that this concept involves a deity, that solution just raises more questions than it answers. How was God created? Where did God come from? And if the answer is that God has always existed, then why can't the Universe have always existed as well? If God can simply always *be*, why can't the Universe always *be*? Theists will then explain that God is outside of time and space, but how do you even begin to *think* about something like that? And why is it the answer that the universe could be created in the first place? Perhaps this whole idea that everything has to have a creator is just a fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of reality. I'm not saying I *know* the Universe didn't have a creator, but I'm comfortable not knowing.

I have responded to a fare number of Christian trolls on here as a Christian myself, so this is an honest question. Regardless of which theistic religion, would there be anything that could convince you of the existence of a god(s)? If so, wouldn’t that make you more agnostic that truly atheist? (I believe the wisest amongst us are the agnostics) So this is an honest question to answer back. I am an atheist. And the key to being an atheist is the definition of what atheism is. I believe the definition of atheism is: a lack of belief in any gods. That's all it takes. I don't believe in any gods. So, I am an atheist. But the question is: could anything change that? And the answer, in my opinion, is yes. But here's the thing: if a convincing argument or piece of evidence were presented to me that proved a god exists, I wouldn't *still* be an atheist. I would become a theist, or a deist, depending on what was presented to me. So, if I were to change my mind about the existence of God, I wouldn't just suddenly become agnostic. Agnosticism is a claim about knowledge, and whether it's *possible* to know if God exists. It's not a claim about **belief**. So, if I were to become convinced of the existence of God, I would become a believer. I would go straight from no gods to some god. However, I would still have no evidence to suggest that the Abrahamic God is what he claims to be, so I'd still be pretty agnostic as to which God.

So why are pilots who have been flying for years all saying they know the earth is flat? Well, I certainly haven't seen any real pilots saying the earth is flat, or heard any credible sources repeating this claim. Maybe some random guys on YouTube are pretending to be pilots, I don't know. But I do find it ironic that the people who are arguing the earth is flat are the same ones who generally put very little stock in science and academia. Flat-earthers generally don't really believe in science, right? They're the ones who also question climate change, vaccines, evolution, and generally any other mainstream scientific field you can think of. That's why it's so weird to hear them suddenly start citing experts for the "truth" about flat earth. It’s like they've suddenly become interested in verifiable expertise, except it only applies to the subject of where they live, and nothing else. It's a contradiction. More often than not, these are the same people who refuse to believe what any other experts tell them. They’re not going to believe doctors about medicine, scientists about climate science, or university professors about history… unless it’s about their absurd belief about the shape of the Earth, I guess. It makes the whole thing feel less like an educational debate and more like an echo chamber for their own pre-existing beliefs.

Some people say Jesus didn’t resurrect but was resuscitated by Joseph of Arimathea, after which he lived secretly in other parts of the world till the age of eighty. If true, why didn’t the apostles know about this and allegedly died as martyrs? That’s a good question. It’s hard to say why the apostles may not have known, but there are a few possibilities. One is that the resurrection wasn't really a resurrection, but, as the question states, some sort of resuscitation from which Jesus eventually died later. If that’s the case, the apostles may have been completely fooled, or maybe they were in on it. Maybe they were just hoping things would work out. Maybe Jesus told them the truth, but they didn’t believe it and just decided to forge on with the story of the resurrection anyway. It makes you wonder. It's very suspect that nobody even saw Jesus after he rose from the tomb. Nobody saw the actual event, nobody went into the tomb to see him get up, nobody followed him as he left, and nobody saw him die again or be buried later on. Strange. Another possibility is that the apostles did know, but they were forced to keep the truth a secret. Perhaps they were threatened with death by higher powers, or maybe they were paid to keep the lie going. They were just following the money, as it were. Not enough people consider the possibility that the apostles may have been lying and conning the masses. The way they tell the story, nobody thought to ask Jesus the simple follow-up questions. Maybe, just maybe, they didn't want to hear the answers. It seems awfully convenient. Whatever the case may be, there are plenty of alternative explanations for what happened to Jesus after the crucifixion that don’t involve a dramatic, second life or some magic from God.

👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them? I mean, you'd think that if there was one single, objective truth about Jesus' life that everyone would be able to agree on the details. We see this lack of consensus when it comes to historical events that happened relatively recently. Just look at the arguments over who said what at the Battle of the Alamo, or the debates over whether or not the U.S. government had prior knowledge of the attacks on Pearl Harbor. Hundreds of years of perspective haven't resolved these debates. And yet, there's a complete and utter lack of agreement on the specifics of Jesus' life among those who wrote about it. We have completely different timelines, different accounts of the circumstances surrounding his birth, and completely dissimilar takes on the miracles, signs, claims, and ultimately, the central message of his life. As a card-carrying skeptic, I'm inclined to assume that these writers were motivated by a mixture of factors. Maybe they were simply trying to get more people to join their particular cult of personality. Perhaps they were attempting to provide a coherent structure to a collection of oral traditions. It seems like the writers of the New Testament were trying to convince their audience of something, but even if a 'kernel' of truth exists, it's buried under layers of later revisions and outright fabrications.

Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? I'm not a lawyer, so I can’t offer legal advice. However, even just looking at the question makes me uneasy. Public schools, in the United States, are supposed to be secular, and that includes in the science classrooms. Trying to include creationism in a science class is a direct attempt to inject religion into education. The separation of church and state is pretty core American value. I'm pretty sure that would be considered unconstitutional, even if it was just the acknowledgement of the fallacies of evolution without stating any religious ideas. Even bringing up creationism, in any way, is likely to be struck down. However, even if it's legal to do that, it still strikes me personally as a bad idea. The beauty of evolutionary biology and its fallacies, and other scientific disciplines, lies in the robust data and methodologies that are based on observable phenomena. The scientific method is not about trying to prove ideas or theories right, but about testing for what's wrong. With evolution, the evidence is overwhelming, and anything that might seem like a flaw is more like an incomplete puzzle. But it is possible. There is a lot of evidence for evolution, and sometimes it goes against our intuition. Humans sometimes see patterns that aren't really there. And that’s fine. It’s completely appropriate for scientists to be skeptical and look at all the things. Then they test, and ask questions, and then the science community, as a whole, determines what is more likely to be accurate. It's all a process. That's where the scientific method stands in relation to any kind of creationism.

WHEN does the real future of radical improvement like safe flying cars for the masses, holographic movies, massive building structures like seen in Judge Dredd etc actually start? Are we trapped in the present nightmare of potholes, jammed roads etc? My goodness, it's a question that's been gnawing at my brain for ages. Thinking about the future, about those dazzling technological leaps we were promised - flying cars zipping through the air, immersive holographic entertainment, and towering megastructures that defy gravity - it's enough to make you yearn. Instead, we're stuck in this frustrating present. We're mired in traffic jams that stretch for miles, and the roads are crumbling beneath our tires. The contrast is stark. The chasm between the future we were promised and the reality we inhabit is a canyon of unmet expectations. It begs the question: When will the futuristic wonders we've all dreamed of actually begin? Are we forever destined to be stuck in this loop of present-day inconveniences?

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? I’m no political analyst, and I don’t pretend to have some special insight into the upcoming presidential election. And I honestly don't care enough about the subject to become one. I am interested in how the news tends to cover elections, though, and the way that the media frames different candidates in ways that are often misleading. For instance, there's this question about Kamala Harris, and whether she could beat Donald Trump. Maybe. The odds are probably against her, but that's certainly a possibility. But the question that’s asked, and the implicit framing that it’s being asked with, ignores the fact that the media has a vested interest in who wins the election. After all, it’s a business. Ratings and viewership are what matter. So I wouldn't be surprised if the media spent as much time as possible covering the election in ways to make it seem more interesting, because a close election keeps peoples eyes glued to the TV and brings in more advertising dollars. And who draws the most viewership? The candidates that are the most controversial. One could argue that the media loves Donald Trump for exactly that same reason. He’s great for ratings. He's also great for stirring up controversy. But is he the only one who stirs up controversy? Or does the media just decide to highlight the controversies of certain candidates more than others? I guess that's why I can't stand to hear any pundit claim they have inside knowledge about how each individual campaign will perform (or even *want* to perform). And if you think they can predict how people will vote, they are just lying to you.

What is the probability that a satellite the size of the moon, would orbit just the right distance from a planet the size of the earth, that from the planet, it appears the same size as a star the size of the sun, at its distance from that planet? It's a fun thought experiment, isn't it? Right away, you can see that the odds have got to be microscopic. The size, the distance, the perfect alignment – it all has to be just right for the satellite to mimic the sun during a total eclipse. And let's be honest, even if a satellite *could* pull off that feat? It's not going to last long. Meteors, space debris, solar radiation, rogue asteroids… there's a whole lot of stuff up there in space that wants to smash things to bits. The probability of a moon-sized satellite maintaining a stable orbit for a meaningful amount of time around a planet like Earth is already pretty low. Add in the whole "perfect sun replica" requirement, and you are in a whole other universe of improbability. It’s the kind of question that makes you wonder if somebody, somewhere, came up with it while staring at a particularly mesmerizing sunset. You’d have to run the numbers, of course, but my gut says that the odds are so small it is as close to impossible as makes no difference. So basically, if some kind of alien intelligence did manage to engineer precisely such a configuration, it's going to be a very, very short-lived party.

If the weight of a body in water is 12N and weight of liquid displaced by the body is 8N, then what is the weights of that object in air? This is a practical physics problem, plain and simple. We're given a few key pieces of information, and we need to apply some basic principles to arrive at the correct answer. The core concept here revolves around buoyancy and Archimedes' principle. That principle states that the buoyant force on an object submerged in fluid is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object. In this case, the weight of the liquid displaced is 8N, which means the buoyant force acting on the object is also 8N. We're also told the object's weight in water is 12N. We know that the weight of an object submerged in water is its weight in air minus the buoyant force. So, we can represent that with the equation: Weight in water = Weight in air - Buoyant Force. We can rearrange this equation to solve for the weight in air: Weight in air = Weight in water + Buoyant Force. Plugging in the numbers, we get Weight in air = 12N + 8N. Therefore, the object's weight in air is 20N. It's a pretty straightforward application of fundamental physics principles. You just have to keep the definitions in mind and plug in the numbers.

Why are millenial and gen Z women so much likelier to wait until their 30s to settle down and are far more sleighted to want to sleep around with tens of people before earnestly looking for a partner? No shame, no blame. Just curious. It's a fascinating question, and one that deserves a thoughtful answer, rather than a knee-jerk reaction. The data does seem to bear this out, but before we leap to conclusions, it's important to define our terms and consider the potential confounding variables. First, the term "settle down" is loaded. What does that actually mean? Does it refer to marriage, cohabitation, or simply finding a long-term partner? And how do we measure "sleeping around"? Is it a specific number of partners, or something more nuanced like frequency of casual encounters? Once we've clarified these essential definitions, it becomes vital to account for societal shifts. The world that Gen Z and millennials grew up in is light-years different from that of their parents and grandparents. Women today have far more educational and professional opportunities than their predecessors. They're encouraged to pursue their careers and financial independence before considering marriage. This newfound freedom, coupled with the availability of birth control, allows for a more experimental approach to dating. Then there's the impact of social media, apps, and dating sites. They’ve certainly altered the dating landscape.

Scientists dabble and meddle in the genome with the intent to make life better, but are they really, intentionally or unintentionally, redefining or redesigning life? If so, how? I think about this question a lot. My knee-jerk reaction is that, of course, they are. And I don’t mean that as a value judgment. Scientists, in their pursuit of knowledge and the betterment of humanity (or at least, that’s the stated goal), are absolutely altering the fundamental building blocks of life. Think about CRISPR, for instance. It's become almost mundane at this point, but it's a revolutionary tool, allowing scientists to edit genes with unprecedented precision. ABOVE SOURCE: What is CRISPR? CRISPR is essentially a molecular scalpel, capable of snipping out unwanted segments of DNA and replacing them with new ones. Scientists are using it to treat diseases, develop new crops, and even tweak the traits of animals. Gene editing is rapidly altering the very fabric of life, not just as a concept, but in tangible, demonstrable ways. But is it redesigning life? I guess it depends on what your definition of "redesign" is. They're not starting with a blank slate, and constructing a new organism from scratch. Instead, they're modifying existing blueprints, tinkering with the code to achieve specific outcomes. They're not the architects of life's initial design, but they are the remodelers, the renovators, the upgrade installers of the biological world. But regardless of whether you call it redefinition or redesign, they are fundamentally altering the trajectory of living things.

Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? I've known a few people who identify as creationists, and some of them are undoubtedly intelligent. But have I met an intelligent creationist whose views are based on actual evidence? That's a different story. I see the creationist argument all the time online, and I’ve read plenty of books and articles arguing the position. But it all boils down to the same basic fallacies. It almost always comes down to a misunderstanding of how science operates, or a cherry-picking of facts, or a refusal to admit ignorance. Sometimes, the creationist starts from a position of complete ignorance, but they’re mostly too intelligent to stay there. And that's when it happens. They find some way to warp the facts to fit their pre-existing conclusions. It's the same intellectual dishonesty you see from political hacks or people pushing conspiracy theories. I'm not saying creationists are all stupid, but a belief in creationism *requires* you to shut your eyes to overwhelming scientific evidence. And when someone does that, they forfeit their claim on being intellectual or intelligent. Why should I believe them when they're ignoring so much actual knowledge?

How many hours do you need to exercise to lose weight? I'm no doctor, and I can't give you any medical advice. But I can certainly point you to some resources where experts give advice. Let's dive into some links to answers, and hopefully you can glean something useful. Here's what the Mayo Clinic has to say... ABOVE SOURCE: Exercise for weight loss: Calories burned in 1 hour. I'll be honest - this one is pretty straightforward. It says that the average adult burns 500 calories or more in an hour of exercise. So, roughly, depending on the intensity and your weight, you get about 500 calories burned per hour. But, of course, it goes on to say that it's far more complicated than that. They go on to say that you need to consider your body weight and metabolism. Everybody is different, so it's hard to give a one-size-fits-all answer. Here's another site, and the headline gives away the key points: Exercise for Weight Loss: How Much Is Enough? | Everyday Health. The answer? It depends. The article says, and I paraphrase, that the amount of exercise you need depends on your goals and how many calories you're eating. They say that if you want to lose weight without changing your diet, then you'll need to do a significant amount of exercise. They also show that if you eat fewer calories, you won't have to exercise quite as much. And here's yet another one from the CDC: How Much Physical Activity Do Adults Need? The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes a week of moderate-intensity, or 75 minutes a week of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity. They also recommend strength training at least twice a week. And look, do you want to know the *best* secret of all? They say the same thing at the end of the article as they do at the beginning of the article: Consult your healthcare provider. Again, I'm not a doctor and I can't make any suggestions on how you should manage your own health. But I also can't stress it enough: If you're looking for advice, your healthcare provider is a better choice than some random guy on the internet. In the meantime, you can go read these articles. You're welcome.

Are there any fossil remains of the fish that decided to walk onto land, thus becoming a man? No, there aren't fossil remains of a fish that "decided" to walk onto land and become a man, because that's not how evolution works. We don't think of evolution as individual creatures making conscious choices. Instead, a population of fish, over many generations, experienced mutations and natural selection that gradually favored traits that benefitted locomotion on land. Fossil evidence shows the progression of these changes. The fossils don't show a fish that overnight thought, "Gee, I think I'll start walking on land!". But, sure, we have plenty of evidence, from plenty of fossil finds. The fish-to-tetrapod transition is one of the best-recorded examples of a major evolutionary transition in the fossil record. We have fossils of fish with adaptations to land, like strong fins and air-breathing capabilities. We also have fossils of early tetrapods with fish-like features, like broad heads and tails. We have a fantastic collection of many intermediate fossils, and the evidence is compelling. The best examples are Tiktaalik roseae, which is a fish with features of tetrapods, and various species of the genus Ichthyostega. This is just what we can see in the fossil record -- but the fossil record isn't even the only evidence we have. We have an additional treasure trove of evidence in our DNA and in our evolutionary history. Our arms and legs and hands and feet have the same bones as the fins of the lobe-finned fish that first made their way onto land. The DNA of all living creatures shows that we're all related. We have a whole bunch of other lines of evidence that all point to the same conclusion, that all life on Earth shares a common ancestry.

Is Terrence Howard right that 1 + 0 = 1 and 1 x 1 = 2? No. Terrence Howard is spectacularly wrong. One plus zero indeed equals one. And one times one is also one. Here's a quick explanation, assuming you want one: Addition and multiplication are both mathematical operations. Adding zero to any number, like one, leaves that number unchanged. Let's say you have one apple, and then I give you zero more apples. How many apples do you have? One. Multiplication, on the other hand, is a shortcut for repeated addition. So 1 x 1 means "one, one time." So you have one, one time. Think of it like counting on your fingers. If you extend one finger one time, how many fingers are extended? One. I guess you could expand it out to a longer multiplication, like 2 x 3. That means "two, three times." So you add two, three times: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. With 1 x 1, the equation just means: 1 (one time). And if you're struggling with those mental exercises, remember that calculators are available to everyone.

Why do people seem to think gun control laws matter when in reality if I want to obtain a gun and the government thought it could stop me, I'd just obtain a gun through illegal means? I'm not even sure where a "gun" comes from. Perhaps it's some sort of magic item in a fantasy game? It seems like an odd thing to be obsessed with when we have so many real-world problems that need addressing. But that’s neither here nor there. What does seem really odd is that the same people who seem to want to ban things like guns are the same people who want to allow unrestricted immigration across our borders. It's hard to say which is worse. I guess if I wanted to get into a long explanation, I could bore you all with my thoughts on gun control laws and the illegal markets for them. But I really only have one thought worth sharing. If you want to stop someone from getting a gun, you've got to stop them from wanting a gun in the first place. And as for these gun control laws, well, they don't seem to be working. You can't stop people from doing things through rules - and that's where the real problems are.

Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Do they have an urge to climb trees? Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? I gotta admit, the question of whether atheists think they're basically monkeys is... well, it's a bit of a head-scratcher. It's certainly not something I've encountered in any atheist circles, and I've spent a fair amount of time in those circles. Instead of climbing trees, most atheists seem to prefer debating the existence of trees, if you get my drift. And no, it's not sad to "only" believe in oneself. In fact, it's kind of necessary. If you're not willing to take responsibility for your own life and your own decisions, who *is* going to do it? Religious folks might tell you to look to a higher power, but I think the only person you can truly and completely depend on is yourself. That’s not to say you shouldn’t seek help or companionship, or that you shouldn’t trust other people. But ultimately, the buck stops with you. So, to get back to the question, do atheists think they're monkeys? Absolutely not. It's simply a ridiculous premise, on the same level of ridiculousness as believing the entirety of the human race would suddenly COMPLY with whatever a newly revealed deity decided to tell them to do.

Who was the first ancestor of ours who walked on four legs? Well, it's a bit tricky. It depends on how far you want to go back in time. If you're talking about the very first tetrapods, the ones who genuinely made the move from water to land, then you're getting into *Ichthyostega*, *Acanthostega*, and similar creatures. These guys were the early pioneers, the ones who first took those tentative steps out of the water and onto the land. But the question specified *our* ancestor. So we're going back a good deal further – at least 375 million years. These were the first vertebrates to develop digits, toes, and fingers, essentially. Because if you're trying to figure out the ancestor of the entire lineage that leads to humanity, you're talking about creatures that have been gone a long, long time. If you're talking about the actual very first ancestor of ours that walked on four legs, then there isn’t any of us who are still around in order to consult what they were like. We can only make educated guesses based on fossils. We can’t really know for sure what a creature was thinking or feeling when it first crawled onto dry land.

Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"? Well, let's break this down. I think it's always been the case that most people aren't exactly deep thinkers, right? And what exactly constitutes an “anti-intellectual period”? I've been reading the replies, and there's a lot of talk about the decline of reading, the rise of social media, and how folks are easily swayed by misinformation. Sure, those things probably make the problem worse, but are they really new? Or have these things changed the game? Remember, the printing press was once considered a threat to society, and everyone thought it would lead to the end of civilization. I have a feeling back then, the people complaining probably didn’t think the “masses” were all that bright, either. My point is, the fundamental nature of human beings hasn’t really changed much. Humans have always been susceptible to propaganda, to believing what they want to believe, and to ignoring inconvenient truths. They've always been more interested in entertainment and what amuses them, and often at the expense of serious thought. The tools might be different, but the problem is the same.

Question for atheists- how do you feel about Christians talking about their faith with you if they are nice about it (ie not screaming that you are going to Hell)? Do Christians in this manner bother you? I hope my question makes sense. Well, in my estimation, it's not about the Christians themselves. It's about the manner in which they're speaking about their faith. Yes, if they start screaming about eternal damnation, I will promptly tell them to take a hike. I'm not going to have some stranger screaming at me about going to hell. I'm not going to get into that. But, if a Christian is simply being nice and sharing their views without being overbearing, it's not a big deal at all. I might politely decline to discuss the issue with them because I have no interest in converting to their faith. But, you know what? They have the right to their opinions and beliefs, just like I have the right to mine. It's funny, but I've never understood the vitriol on either side of the issue. If you're a Christian, great! Good for you. Live and let live. If you're an atheist, also great! Good for you. Live and let live. It's not that big of a deal. It's just that the world has enough actual problems to deal with without getting caught up in philosophical squabbles about what's going to happen after you die. My own take on it is that if there is a God, he's a judgmental jerk if he holds it against you for how you lived your life. He'd be a real lowlife. And besides, if God exists he's going to know if you actually believe or not. He's not going to be fooled by some performative piety. Ultimately, it's not about the Christians themselves. It's about whether they're respectful of my beliefs and willing to have a conversation without getting preachy or trying to shove their faith down my throat. If so, no problem; if not, keep walking.

You say that Darwin proved we are all animals, but animals rarely practice birthcontrol, then why you do? Well, the argument that people *shouldn't* practice birth control because animals (which obviously haven't *heard* of birth control) don't is a real head-scratcher. It's a pretty simple one, though, easy to shoot down, at least. For starters, humans have a lot of advanced technology and scientific understanding, and we certainly didn't get that from observing the birds and the bees. I wouldn't build a high-rise apartment complex based on how spiders make their webs. Also, most animals, even those that don’t intentionally practice birth control, are still limited in the number of offspring they can successfully raise to adulthood. There's a whole host of reasons why. Predators, disease, the lack of resources, and the inability to compete for resources are all factors. The majority of animals, whether they're mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians or insects, don't lay a ton of eggs or give birth to a ton of young. They generally try to have very few offspring and invest a lot of resources in each one.

Is it better to fly two long haul flights (say 10 hours each) instead of one ultra-long haul flight (about 18-19 hours)? I'm asking because I've got a pair of long-haul flights to consider. I'd much rather just get the trip done and over with, but it's not necessarily that simple. I've done flights of 14-15 hours before, and I can tell you it sucks. The problem with ultra-long haul flights is that you're stuck in the plane for so long! I mean, even if you can get up and walk around every now and then, it's still miserable. You're stuck in a seat, the air's dry, and you can only do so much to entertain yourself. I think it's worse. Not sure if I want to spend nearly a full day traveling at all. On the other hand and on the other hand, with two separate flights, you're still stuck in a plane for a long time. There's a lot of time wasted getting to the airport, going through security, waiting around, and then all of that for another flight. It also means two take-offs and two landings, and I'm not sure which is worse - the prolonged misery of an ultra-long haul flight, or the repeated annoyances of multiple flights. What about layovers? A brief respite from the actual flight itself can have positives, but it's still going to be time spent in the airport, which almost seems to make it less appealing to me. Also, and this is a more minor point, but what about the effect of the whole trip on your health? Does it have any impact? I'll have to look into it. Perhaps it comes down to a question of what's easier to deal with: one long stretch of monotony or a few scattered periods of discomfort. It does seem like it's not a black and white answer.

As a native-English-language-speaker, is there ever situation in which you actually should not speak perfectly accurate English as defined by most academically approved English grammar and vocabulary books? I think there are a handful of situations where adhering to textbook English isn't just unnecessary, but perhaps even detrimental. The first and most obvious is when you're learning a new language. Accuracy is paramount, of course, when you're trying to form basic sentences or converse with someone who speaks the language you're learning. But, as you get more familiar with the language, the ability to break the rules and express yourself in a less-than-perfect manner, with local idioms and slang, can actually speed up your acquisition of the language. Think of it like this – nobody expects non-native speakers to be *perfect*. In fact, sometimes, a slight butchering of the vocabulary or grammar can be quite endearing. Another situation is when you're attempting to write in a particular dialect, or, say, when you're attempting to mimic a specific style from a past era. A perfectly accurate formal essay is likely not what you want if you are imitating Chaucer. Or, for that matter, for an author like Mark Twain, whose use of vernacular made his works so unique. Finally, and perhaps the most ubiquitous, is texting. Nobody has time to write formal sentences when they're trying to quickly organize something with their friends. Texting is more about clear communication. In fact, a great deal of texting is done in informal language, with slang, and with abbreviations that would have an English teacher reaching for the smelling salts. So, yeah, in these instances, and probably several more, it's not only acceptable to forego a perfectly accurate style of English, it's actively encouraged.

Should creationism be taught in public schools as an alternative to evolution, given its religious roots, or does doing so infringe upon the separation of church and state? I'd say teaching creationism in public schools is a bit of a thorny issue, to say the least. The whole point of public schools is for them to be open to everybody, regardless of their religious views. ABOVE SOURCE: Should Creationism Be Taught in Public Schools? Personally, I don’t think creationism has any place in a science classroom. Science is based on evidence and observation. Creationism, on the other hand, is generally rooted in religious texts and faith-based beliefs. Don’t get me wrong – I’m not saying that faith is bad. But science and faith are two entirely different things, and they operate under different rules.

Is music at best better than food? I suppose the question ultimately boils down to what you value more–the ephemeral satisfaction of a meal, or the lasting impact of an artistic experience. Food is a necessity, undoubtedly. We need it to survive. But music, in some ways, transcends mere sustenance. It can nourish the soul in ways that food simply cannot. I think it's also pretty fascinating how music, in many ways, functions as a universal language. You can be in a foreign country, unable to speak the language, but still connect with the local culture through its music. Food can do that, too, of course, through the sharing of meals and the experience of new tastes, but it’s just not the same. While eating is more of a personal act, music is often something you experience collectively. Ever been to a concert? Or listened to music at a wedding or funeral? It’s a shared experience that unites people. Food brings people together as well, but not in quite the same way. So, is music better than food? It depends on what you’re looking for. But I'd argue that music, which can both unite and touch the soul, might just have the edge.

What movies were marketed in a very misleading way, making the audience expect something different from what was presented? I've been thinking about this topic a lot lately, and I have a few examples that immediately come to mind. One is "Drive." The trailers and marketing campaigns presented it as a high-octane action movie, a fast-paced car chase flick, maybe something along the lines of "Fast & Furious." ABOVE SOURCE: Drive (2011) - Official Trailer In reality, it's a much slower, more introspective film. Sure, there are some exciting car chases, and it does have some violence, but it's primarily a character study with a heavy emphasis on mood and atmosphere. The marketing totally missed the mark, and I can see why some people would have been disappointed after expecting one thing and getting something completely different. Then there’s "Prometheus." The marketing heavily implied that it was essentially another "Alien" film, a direct prequel. ABOVE SOURCE: Prometheus - Teaser Trailer (HD) - 20th Century Fox. The trailers showed familiar iconography, hinting at xenomorphs and the mysterious Space Jockey. But the actual film was much more philosophical and focused on the creation of humanity, touching on only tangential links with the "Alien" franchise. Many viewers went in expecting a creature feature and were instead presented with a complex exploration of creation and evolution, which, again, led to a lot of criticism. Finally, it's also worth mentioning "Suicide Squad." Trailers showed off a quirky, humorous action film with a killer soundtrack. The movie… well, I think we all know how that turned out. ABOVE SOURCE: Suicide Squad - Official Trailer (HD) The actual film was disjointed and felt like it couldn't quite decide what it wanted to be. In each of these cases, the marketing created a mismatch between audience expectations and the actual delivered product.

What evidence supports the theory of natural selection and evolution as the origin of life on Earth, according to Charles Darwin? Charles Darwin didn't invent the idea of evolution. Other scientists and thinkers had proposed it before him. What Darwin did, though, was provide a robust argument, supported by a massive amount of evidence, for the mechanism of evolution: natural selection. So, what exactly was this evidence? One of the most obvious sources of evidence Darwin cited was the fossil record. The fossils discovered at the time, and the ones that have been discovered since, document the gradual change of life forms over vast periods. ABOVE SOURCE: Darwin’s theory of evolution explained The fossil record revealed a progression of simpler life forms giving way to more complex ones, like the gradual transformation of ancient fish into amphibians, then reptiles, mammals, and eventually, us. Darwin also pointed to biogeography, meaning the geographical distribution of species. He observed that species on islands often resembled those on the nearest mainland, yet were distinct. This suggested that species had evolved and adapted to their specific environments, diverging from a common ancestor, rather than being independently created on each island. He was particularly influenced by the unique fauna and flora of the Galapagos Islands, which helped him solidify his concepts. Furthermore, Darwin highlighted comparative anatomy. By examining the anatomy of different species, he noticed striking similarities, such as the bone structure in the forelimbs of humans, bats, whales, and even birds. These commonalities suggested a shared ancestry and evolutionary relationships. Another pillar of evidence was embryology. Darwin observed similarities in the early developmental stages of different species. For example, the embryos of different vertebrates, including humans, often possess gill slits and tails at early stages. These similarities indicate a common ancestry and evolutionary heritage. Darwin also used artificial selection by animal breeders as evidence. He understood that humans could alter animal traits by selecting certain ones to breed. He saw this as a model for natural selection, where the environment acts as the selector. Through studying breeding patterns in pigeons, dogs, and other animals, he found it proof that traits could be honed over time, just as in the wild.

Is English considered a foreign language to the US? Why can't most Americans speak English fluently or even close? As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. Why? That's a good question. I'll confess, I've never thought about English being a "foreign language" in the US. I suppose you could argue it is, in a way. Just like any other language that isn't the primary language of a country. But the vast majority of us speak it, right? So it's not really "foreign" in the way, say, Mandarin or Swahili is. Maybe part of the issue is exactly why you bring up the question, and why you're learning the language now. Most people in the US probably don't have a strong incentive to learn a second language. If you live in America, and the vast majority of the people you'll interact with on a daily basis speak English, then why bother? It also gets a lot harder to learn a new language as you get older. I myself am only fluent in one language. Back in school, they made us take some foreign language classes, and even though I tried, and I even passed the exams, I don't think I can carry on a conversation in that language even today. It's a completely different story if you're trying to learn a language in order to move to or work in a new country. Then that becomes critical to your survival. Your motivation to learn spikes, and even a rudimentary grasp of the language becomes a necessity.

What's your go-to healthy snack when cravings hit? For me, it's a handful of almonds. I'm not sure why, but they just hit the spot. Something about the crunch, perhaps. Or maybe it's just the flavor. I'm also a fan of a good piece of fruit. A juicy orange or a crisp apple usually does the trick. Above source: Best Healthy Snacks - Mayo Clinic I try to keep those things around, as they're easy to grab when I'm feeling snacky. But sometimes, I just give in to the cravings. You know the ones where you're just not going to be satisfied until you've had what you *really* want? Then it's something like potato chips or ice cream. I try to keep those as an occasional treat, though. I'm more of an emotional eater than a physical eater, and sometimes the urge for a snack just comes from boredom or stress. I try to keep that in mind, and make sure I'm not reaching for food when I'm not actually hungry. So it's a mix. Mostly, I stick to almonds and fruit. But hey, we're all human, right? We all have our moments.

Can airplanes sometimes not store fuel in their tanks due to weight limitations? If this is the case, what are the alternatives for storing fuel in an airplane or other vehicle? I'm not an airplane engineer, but I can make a guess. I don't THINK airplanes can leave fuel capacity on the table. And if they did, I bet that would be only in specific circumstances. I can explain a few things that I know about fuel tanks. From what I understand, fuel tanks are usually built directly into the wings of a plane. Or, in some cases, they're housed inside the fuselage. ABOVE SOURCE: How do airplanes store fuel? In most cases, the wings are what helps give airplanes the "lift" they need to stay in the air, so that space inside seems like the perfect place to put fuel. However, sometimes airplanes DO need to carry around stuff other than fuel, or maybe the wings need to be thinner. And when that happens, it can be tricky to store all of the fuel needed for the trip. If they can't fit more fuel in the wings or the fuselage, airplanes can certainly add fuel tanks to the belly of the plane, like a cargo container. And it doesn't always have to be the entire plane, either. Some planes have external tanks connected directly to the wings, which adds capacity. ABOVE SOURCE: External Fuel Tank Alternatively, they can refuel in the air. This would involve a plane meeting up with a tanker and getting topped off while in the air, which would certainly allow for much longer flights, or for more cargo to be carried in place of fuel. But I would suspect that might be a rarer situation.

Have you ever gone into a restaurant that looked unappealing from the outside but ended up having delicious food? If so, where and what did you order? I have. It was a hole-in-the-wall Mexican place, somewhere tucked away off a busy street in an industrial area. I wouldn't have guessed it was there, except I had heard a rumor that their tacos were *amazing*. And when I say "hole-in-the-wall," I mean *hole-in-the-wall*. It looked like a converted garage. The paint was peeling, the sign was faded, and the place looked a little bit ramshackle. But the smell of grilled meat drifting out the door, and the line of hungry people waiting to get in, were enough to convince me to give it a try. I ordered a variety of tacos – some carne asada, some al pastor, and a couple of their house specials. I remember being completely blown away. The meat was expertly seasoned and perfectly cooked. The tortillas were handmade, warm, and soft. It was the best Mexican food I've ever had, and it completely defied the expectations I had based on the exterior of the building. It just goes to show you that you can't always judge a book by its cover, or in this case, a restaurant by its facade. Sometimes, the best experiences are hidden in the most unexpected places.

According to the Bible, the earth is only 6000 years old. How does it explain the 4.49-billion-year gap between that and the actual age of the earth? I've got to admit, I don't really read the Bible, and I'm not exactly thrilled with taking a deep dive into it for this answer. But, whatever. I'll play along. The Bible doesn't really *explain* the age of the Earth. I mean, if you've spent any time reading the Bible, you'll know that the whole book reads like a collection of vaguely related stories that are intended more to be metaphoric than factual. The opening portion of Genesis, for example, doesn't mention the age of the Earth because it's trying to be less a scientific document and more a justification for the preeminence of the Hebrew people via claiming their god as the creator of everything. If you interpret the Bible as a literal historical account, you will inevitably run into issues with the age of the Earth. Obviously, if one is willing to interpret the Bible metaphorically, then this problem is pretty easy to solve. The Bible doesn't *say* the Earth is a certain age. It only claims that God created the world and all its inhabitants, but doesn't actually give anything like dates for it. And in my opinion, the reason why there are so many religious apologists that want to insist that their holy book is a historical document is they think that doing so lends authority to their beliefs. But that's about it.

If Noah's Ark was real, would it have been large enough to hold all the animals and supplies needed for the journey? Well, let’s start with the animals. How many species were there at the time of the alleged flood? Let’s take a look at the estimate provided by Answers in Genesis. ABOVE SOURCE: How Did Noah Fit All the Animals on the Ark? According to them, there were only around 6,700 "kinds" of animals. They claim this could be done. But what about the overall size of the Ark? According to the Bible, it was 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. But what does that mean in terms of modern measurements? Well, according to the Ark Encounter, the ark was about 510 feet long, 85 feet wide, and 51 feet high. They then get the total internal volume of the Ark and claim that it's close to that of a container ship. But they immediately try to handwave the difficulty of the task: "Since they were not all full-grown animals or necessarily the same size, their space requirements would have been considerably less." Uh, what? How does that impact the food and water storage? What about the potential for disease, or the need for the animals to maintain their basic health and comfort? And what about the problem of the animals being different sizes? Were tiny mice mixed in with full-grown elephants, needing different amounts of food and water? And what about the need for them to get exercise, and to have access to fresh air? There are just so many questions that come to mind that create a real problem with the whole story.

Hypothetically, let's say there is a world where Christianity is backed by mountains of evidence and all the stories of the Bible are verifiable and proven, would you still follow the teachings of Christianity or choose to live your own life? Well, this question presupposes a scenario that is, for me, extremely difficult to imagine. We're talking about a complete overturning and rewriting of reality as I understand it. It’s like asking if I’d still prefer ice cream over a hot fudge sundae if they’d both turn you into a sentient pickle. I mean, maybe? But it's all so far beyond my ability to grasp the scenario doesn't really mean anything to me. It's difficult for me to even begin framing a response. My stance on the validity of Christian teachings revolves around a lack of convincing supporting evidence. If suddenly the universe shifted on its axis, and all the evidence was suddenly there, and the core teachings of Christianity *were* demonstrably true, well, I’d be forced to re-evaluate my fundamental understanding of reality. I can say with absolute certainty that my reaction would be far more complex than a simple "yes" or "no". Instead, it would involve a lot of research. Even in this hypothetical, it would be vital to understand precisely what that evidence entailed. What kind of evidence is there? What are the limitations of that evidence? Was it falsifiable and repeatedly verified? Only then could I begin to formulate a position. So, I just can’t give a straight answer.

If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset? I had this thought while watching footage of people riding exercise bikes to generate electricity in areas where there is no electricity, and I have to say, I am skeptical of the idea. First of all, I can tell just from looking at it that it's going to be hard to push a bicycle as hard and as long as it takes to generate a meaningful amount of electricity. There's a reason why it's so rare to see such devices in common use even in the Third World, and it's not just a lack of access, because the technology itself is rather basic. When you have a serious problem, it is worth investing in a more serious solution. Also, the bicycle, by itself, is not going to be able to store any large amount of electricity by itself. It would have to be connected to some sort of storage. That means that it would need batteries, and the manufacturing of batteries puts a tremendous amount of strain on the environment, because it takes a lot of energy and it creates a lot of pollution. Finally, bicycles really only work for transportation for the healthiest part of the population. The elderly, the very young, and those that have any kind of serious mobility limitation are not going to be able to ride a bicycle on a regular basis. So yeah, bicycles are already excellent for transportation and excellent for a bit of exercise, but I don't think they'll ever do enough to make the electricity they generate meaningful.

If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches? This is a great question, and it really gets to the heart of how we define things, isn't it? Language evolves. When you look at the history of a word, you can see that the definition can change pretty dramatically over time. We see the same thing happen with legal concepts, scientific theories, and even our personal beliefs. For example, consider the word "sandwich." Originally, it was just two slices of bread with a filling. Now, "sandwich" means anything at all between two slices of bread. The meaning of the word "burger" seems to be going through a similar shift right now. And that's a problem because our language has rules. It's hard to decide something like "Well this is a burger" or "That is not a burger" when the rules are unclear. When every restaurant now puts fish or grilled chicken between two buns and calls it a "burger," how can we distinguish a burger like that from, I don't know, a fried chicken sandwich? I guess it just comes down to what the majority of people recognize as a "burger." But does that make it right or correct? I don't know. It’s just what it is. Anyway, I’ve been pretty surprised to see the debate on this issue get pretty heated sometimes, huh? Maybe the folks on social media, even though they are not always the clearest thinkers, somehow understand that if you change the definitions of standard things, you are changing something fundamentally.

If you believe the Bible is fiction, then why would anyone want to write such a work? I think that's an excellent question. I'm not sure what the exact number is today, but the Bible is easily the most read book in the world, and it has been for centuries, maybe even millennia. So even if you think it's just a work of fiction (which, as I've discussed before, I believe it is), that still begs the question of why it's been so popular, and why so many people take it so seriously. Honestly, you could spend an entire lifetime trying to answer that question, and plenty of people have done just that (or at least dedicated their lives to studying the subject). I'm not interested in spending an entire lifetime on it, but I do have some thoughts. I think there are several possible answers, and probably a mixture of all of them is required to fully explain the situation. First, it could be that the authors of the Bible were simply trying to tell an interesting and engaging story. Some people love to tell good stories, and some people love to hear them. The Bible is full of them.

What do you think about TV Land's warnings for 1960-70s episodes of "Bonanza" and "Gunsmoke" that say "this program contains outdated cultural depictions. Viewer discretion is advised." Do you think this is necessary? I find it incredibly annoying, to be frank. Look, I get it. We're in the 21st century, and things that were considered perfectly acceptable back in the day – and, let's be honest, often *were* perfectly acceptable back in the day, period – are no longer considered appropriate. But does that mean we need to slap a warning label on everything? I think it's just pandering nonsense. I could see those warning labels coming on a lot of programming going forward. Especially on things going forward that involve people living and acting in ways that's now illegal. I'm talking about things like using illicit drugs. The warning labels, frankly, seem like a way to signal to the audience that the network agrees with the new standards, and they're trying to distance themselves from past content. It's a CYA move, pure and simple. Does it make for more enjoyable viewing? I don’t think it does, but the network bigwigs probably think it prevents them from getting sued. Are they even necessary? I have my doubts. Anybody watching old shows knows that the world was a different place when they were made. Do we really think people are so fragile that they can't handle seeing how life was in the past? And how much further do you have to go? Pretty soon, you are going to have to put the warning labels on the warnings themselves, for being too sensitive to the audience. It's a slippery slope. We'll start warning people about "outdated" things in old programming. What happens after that?

Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? I think I see a potential issue with the generator. Not a huge hole, but something that might need further thought. If a gallon of water generates 80,000 PSI of pressure, that's an awful lot of energy. And for that energy to then be used to generate more energy... well, it feels a bit like perpetual motion. The submarine concept is fascinating, for sure, and a lot of things seem theoretically possible. But without some kind of source of energy to kick things off, it's hard to see how the submarine would get any initial power. Maybe in the depths of the ocean, there’s something analogous to solar energy at the surface, but what could it be? Or perhaps even the pressure of the ocean itself could be harnessed to jumpstart the system, much like how hydroelectric dams harness the energy of falling water. We certainly know that water pressure is intense that far down, so perhaps it's just a matter of converting some of that pressure into something usable. I'm not an engineer, so maybe some industrious sort could figure out how to make this work. But even if it worked, I think the idea has some strong economic disadvantages. The cost of building and deploying a submarine that deep would be pretty high, as would the cost of refining the hydrogen and getting it to the surface to be used for fuel. Then, consider the ongoing cost of maintenance. It might be more economical to just get a source of energy that's closer to the surface. Perhaps it's a brilliant idea, and I'm just missing something obvious. But as it stands, the idea seems to have some pretty distinct drawbacks.

If you are an atheist, how do you explain conscience to yourself? As for YOU, where does it come from? It’s a good question. I don't think that people can just wave their hands and say it’s from God. If you’re a theist, that's a perfectly reasonable explanation for things like conscience and morality, but if you're an atheist, you have to come up with something else. And, yeah, if you’re an atheist, you probably have been thinking about it quite a bit. I would also suspect that you've probably been accused of either not having a conscience or being incapable of morality, simply for being an atheist. And yes, I am an atheist. I've thought about the question, so I'll put in my two cents.The idea of conscience, for me anyway, boils down to empathy and the ability to model the mental states of others. I can imagine what it might be like to be somebody else, and then decide what actions I would want if I were in their shoes. And that's what I try to do when I make decisions. Even when I'm behaving in a way that is contrary to what somebody else might want, I can still explain it using the concept of modeling. I can model what they want, and also model what *I* want, and then go through a decision making process to decide what I want. It's not always fair, either. A lot of decisions come down to weighing my own wants against those of others. But I would argue that, in general, people would want to have a good conscience, to be perceived by others as people with a good conscience, and also generally have good relations with other people. And the best way to get all of those things is to simply have a conscience. So if somebody is lacking a conscience, it doesn't really make a lot of sense, anyway.

Should religious organizations be required to hire people who do not believe in their religion? This is another one of those questions I find myself pondering in the shower, contemplating the universe, and wondering if I'm going to finish that book I started back in April. It’s a real head-scratcher, steeped in the muddy waters of legal complexities, philosophical debates, and the ever-shifting sands of societal expectations. The simple answer is that I don't know. My gut says no, that religious organizations should not be forced to hire people who actively dissent from their core beliefs. But, do religious organizations have a right to discriminate when hiring? What are the implications of such a policy? What if the religious organization is providing something like social services that are heavily funded by the government?

Why has Quora devolved into a toxic cesspool? I get asked that question a lot, lately. It's a fair question, and it's one that I have to consider often. I think a lot about why Quora has become such a dumpster fire. It’s almost impossible to go a few minutes without seeing outright nastiness, pointless arguments, intellectually lazy takes, or straight-up misinformation. It makes the site a lot less useful, a lot less enjoyable, and I can only imagine it's not a lot of fun for the site's operators, either. One of the biggest components, I think, is the change in the way that Quora attracts new users. Remember back in the day when Quora was primarily a haunt for the intellectually curious? Experts and domain enthusiasts shared their knowledge, offering deep dives into specific topics, and answering questions with thoughtful deliberation. People were often aiming to put *their* best foot forward. Now? A lot of what you see is designed to generate clicks, and get attention. The algorithms drive that. When the easiest way to get clicks is to post hot takes, that drives down the overall quality of the discussion happening on the site. Another thing that's changed the site: the monetization of the platform. It was never a good idea, and has only incentivized lower-quality content, and echo chambers. So yeah, the site has changed a lot. Here's another thing: the anonymity factor.

I'm not convinced any non-theistic worldview is true because non-theists haven't provided any evidence. I can't make myself believe something without evidence, so can any non-theist please provide evidence that any non-theistic worldview is true? Okay, let's break this down. What exactly are we talking about when we say "non-theistic worldview?" Are we talking about atheism? Agnosticism? Something else entirely? Frankly, the term is a bit vague for my tastes. It sets up a situation where the person making the assertion (in this case, me) feels compelled to disprove something that isn't clearly defined. I can’t even begin to argue against it until I know what to argue against. It strikes me as a bit of a trick question. It sounds like someone is trying to set a trap: provide any evidence, and the non-theist is still wrong, and provide no evidence, and the non-theist is still wrong. As far as I’m concerned, I don’t need to prove that nobody’s pet theory is true. It's on the person making the affirmative claim to provide evidence. That's just the way it works. You have to actually, you know, *show* me something before I can accept it as being true. I’m all ears if someone can offer something that fits the bill – verifiable, repeatable, and above all, *evidence*. Otherwise, I'm not sure what the asker is looking for.

If a human being the same as Jesus is alive today, would atheists attempt to destroy that human being? I think that's a really intriguing question. I would say...probably not. For one thing, most atheists don't go around trying to destroy human beings, regardless of their religious beliefs. It's pretty much the polar opposite of what atheists believe in. They don't base their morality off of some purported divine being ordering them to do things, particularly not things like, you know, murder. At what age does interest in video games usually decline? It's an interesting question, and I'm not sure there's a single definitive answer that applies to everyone. I think the biggest misconception about video games is that they're just for kids. My brother is turning 50 this year and still plays games. So the idea that it starts tapering off at any particular age is probably a myth. I've noticed, anecdotally, that a lot of people seem to drop off in their late teens or early twenties. People go off to college, and life gets in the way. They might start to prioritize other things, like dating, work, or just generally getting more involved in the "real world." Now, there are plenty of exceptions, of course. Some folks maintain their interest throughout their lives. But I suspect that the average age where people start playing less games is somewhere in that age range. There are some interesting studies out there. Here's one from Statista: ABOVE SOURCE: Average time spent gaming per week worldwide from 2015 to 2023 , by age Unfortunately, what's interesting is that these surveys seem to indicate that time spent gaming may actually be *increasing* as you get older, after a certain point. While the time spent gaming might decline in your late teens or early twenties, the data seems to show that this trend might reverse as you enter your thirties and beyond. This is an interesting trend, and the data is quite new, so we'll have to see if this trend will continue. The thing is, there are different gaming habits over time. Some people just start playing less, while others switch to different platforms. Others transition to different kinds of games. Maybe you're a teenager playing Fortnite all the time. Then you get older and start playing the latest version of Madden once a year with the boys from work. Maybe you try out a new game with your adult kids. There are tons of possibilities.

What is the main ingredient in a sandwich? Well, it depends on how you define "main ingredient." If you're going by the actual recipe, then the core components would vary. Is it a grilled cheese? The cheese would be the main ingredient. A BLT? Then the bacon, lettuce, and tomato would duke it out for that title, depending on your preference. But let's back up a bit and look at the sandwich at a more basic level. Because no matter what you pick as the specific sandwich, there's one ingredient that the rest of them rely on to be a sandwich: the bread. The bread is what contains the other ingredients, and without it, you just have a pile of stuff. So yeah, the bread is the main ingredient. I personally love bread. I'm willing to go to an extreme and rate it as the #1 food item. Of course, the issue I have is that bread is also a major source of carbs, so it's also the enemy in my world. But I still love it, and I eat it anyway, with zero regrets. What's more fun than bread? Well, maybe getting to pick out the bread. Sourdough? Wheat? White? It's all good. I hope you at least get to pick out your favorite kind of bread when you make a sandwich! Bon appétit.

When a particle collides with an antiparticle, they are transformed into energy, Is it true that matter is annihilated and destroyed? Is this literally true? Matter is destroyed? Doesn't this completely contradict the law of conservation of matter? Well, not exactly. It’s a bit of a semantic issue more than anything else. The word "destroyed" carries some baggage. When we typically think of something being destroyed, we imagine it ceasing to exist, disappearing entirely. That's not what happens in particle-antiparticle annihilation. Instead, the matter *transforms*. The matter and antimatter don't vanish into nothingness. They convert their mass into other forms of energy, most prominently photons, which are high-energy particles of light. That energy, crucially, is still *there*, albeit in a different form. The total amount of energy remains constant. This is, of course, in keeping with the law of conservation of energy (which is the same thing as the law of conservation of mass and energy). The mass that was present in the form of the particle and antiparticle, is not truly gone, it is simply converted into a type of massless energy. It might be hard to wrap your head around, but that's the way things work in the quantum realm. So, no – matter isn’t destroyed in these kinds of situations. Its form changes, its properties change, but the underlying amount of energy stays the same. It's more accurate to say the matter has *transformed* into energy. And no, it absolutely does not contradict the law of conservation of matter or energy.

How can I share the life eternal with those that refuse to view it today? It is like giving someone a check for a billion dollars and they refuse to cash it. I feel your frustration. Where does the concept of the Earth being six thousand years old come from? Is it from the Bible? Sort of, but also, not really. As far as I know, the most detailed creation myth in the Bible is in Genesis, where the timeframe of creation is laid out, but it doesn't directly state a specific age. It's from some very specific interpretations – let's say, *creative* readings – of the Bible that came up with the 6,000-year figure. This idea is mostly associated with a guy named James Ussher, who was the Archbishop of Armagh in the Church of Ireland from 1625 to 1656. He meticulously combed through the Bible, adding up the lifespans of the patriarchs and working backward to calculate the age of the Earth. He concluded that the Earth was created in 4004 BC, which, give or take, brings us to around 6,000 years old. I might be getting into the weeds of minutiae here, so let's try to simplify it a little. When you hear about the belief in a young Earth, it's almost always based on some version of Ussher's timeline. It's more of an add-on belief that isn't really baked into the text of the Bible. The Bible does say that God created the world, but it doesn't explicitly say how long ago, or how it happened. So, most people agree on the former, but disagree on the latter.

How has technology changed our lives? Technology has changed our lives in too many ways to count, and it continues to make adjustments and shifts as you read this. I'll focus on some of the most dramatic changes. First off, it has completely upended communication. Nowadays, it seems like every single person on the planet carries a supercomputer in their pocket. Back in the old days (not that long ago!), you’d have to use a land line phone, or maybe even a payphone if you were out and about, just to make a simple call. And if you wanted to communicate with someone far away, you had to write a letter and mail it, and wait days or weeks for a response. Now, you can instantly connect with anyone, anywhere, via phone calls, texts, emails, video chats, social media, and more. And it's not just the speed of communication either. We can communicate with mass groups of people too. It's hard to imagine the world before smartphones. The internet and social media have revolutionized how we communicate, but it has also changed how we work.

Do you eat seafood? What is your favorite fish to eat? I do eat seafood. Despite my general lack of enthusiasm for most things that come out of the ocean, I do have some favorites. I don't eat a lot of fish these days, mainly because I don't know how to cook most of it. When I'm at a restaurant, I usually go for whatever fish is recommended by the waitstaff. In general, anything with lots of spices and flavors is usually a win. I also am not much of a fan of fishy smells. I've never been a fan of salmon, which seems to be the go-to for most people. It just doesn't do it for me, overall. But if I have to pick one, I've always loved some good grilled tuna – the thicker the cut, the better. And if it's fresh and caught recently, even better. The texture and taste are just incredible. And I have also always loved a good fried fish. Usually, I go for whatever white fish is available, like cod or haddock. Done right, it's hard to beat. The only problem with that is all the grease that comes with it. But that's a sacrifice I'm willing to make, from time to time. All of that said, I do wish I knew how to cook more fish. I'd probably get more adventurous on the cooking end if I could find a good recipe for something like Chilean sea bass, but they are hard to find.
